intro: A dollar of new spending becomes someone's income, and they spend part of it (the MPC), and so on. Explore shows those rounds adding up: the spending multiplier for purchases, the smaller tax multiplier for taxes, and both together. Close a gap shows the routine the exam scores: find the gap, decide the direction, then divide the gap by the multiplier. Money shows how banks lend out excess reserves in the limited-reserves model, and the most the money supply can change.
howItWorks:
• MPS = 1 − MPC.
  • Spending multiplier = 1 ÷ MPS. It applies to a change in government purchases, investment or any other spending.
  • Tax multiplier = −MPC ÷ MPS: negative (a tax rise lowers spending) and one smaller in size, because only the MPC share of a tax change is spent in the first round.
  • Purchases and taxes rising by the same amount change real GDP by that amount (the two effects added).
  • Closing a gap: direction first (a recessionary gap needs more aggregate demand), then policy change = gap ÷ multiplier. Multiplying the gap is the most common slip.
  • Money multiplier (limited reserves) = 1 ÷ required reserve ratio. The largest change in the money supply = excess reserves × money multiplier; a Fed purchase from the public also adds the new deposits themselves, and a cash deposit adds nothing at first.
  • These are the largest changes, in the simple model with a constant price level. With ample reserves, the Fed sets its policy rate with administered rates instead.
